title: Gauging the Conviction of Those Who Advocate
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article cautions leaders against assuming that every proposal or piece of advocacy comes backed by full conviction. The author observes that team members and salespeople often argue forcefully for ideas they only partly believe in, or that they haven't fully developed yet, which can mislead leaders who evaluate arguments purely on their surface strength. The recommended fix is to directly ask advocates to quantify their conviction — on a percentage or numeric scale — rather than inferring commitment from passion or polish alone. The piece extends this to draft materials, urging leaders to confirm whether a proposal or deck is an early or late-stage draft before judging it on its merits.
points: Not all forceful advocacy reflects full conviction in the underlying idea.
Leaders risk being misled by the strength of an argument rather than the advocate's actual confidence in it.
Directly asking advocates to quantify their conviction on a numeric scale reveals more than passion alone.
The same caution applies to draft proposals and decks, which may be early and underdeveloped.
Simple direct questions about certainty are recommended as the most reliable way to gauge true conviction.
quotes: In reality, those who are highly convicted about an answer or an idea are the exception, not the rule.

Gauging the conviction of those who advocate for a proposal or idea helps leaders assess exactly how they should respond and whether they should support or reject the idea at this point in its articulation.
Sixty or even 80 percent confidence is a far cry from 100 percent.
People often propose ideas they suspect are impractical, unworkable, or missing something important. Good leaders don’t fall for it.
Understanding the level of conviction advocates hold is critical to processing the information accurately.
